question: There are integers \(a\) and \(b\) such that the polynomial \(x^3 - 5x^2 + ax + b\) has \(4 + \sqrt{5}\) as a root. What is \(a + b?\)
solution:
The integer coefficients force \(4-\sqrt5\) to be another root. Pairing these roots gives a simple quadratic factor, and evaluating at \(1\) will reveal \(a+b\) directly.

Let
\[
P(x)=x^3-5x^2+ax+b.
\]
To justify the conjugate root, expanding \(P(4+\sqrt5)\) produces an expression \(U+V\sqrt5\), where \(U,V\) are integers. This expression is zero. If \(V\ne0\), then \(\sqrt5=-U/V\) would be rational, so \(U=V=0\). Replacing \(\sqrt5\) by \(-\sqrt5\) in the expansion gives \(P(4-\sqrt5)=U-V\sqrt5=0\).

The two roots give the factor
\[
(x-4-\sqrt5)(x-4+\sqrt5)
=(x-4)^2-5=x^2-8x+11.
\]
By the factor theorem, the monic cubic therefore has the form
\[
P(x)=(x^2-8x+11)(x-r)
\]
for its remaining root \(r\). The coefficient of \(x^2\) in this product is \(-8-r\), so
\[
-8-r=-5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=-3.
\]
Now evaluate at \(1\):
\[
P(1)=(1-8+11)(1+3)=16.
\]
Also, \(P(1)=1-5+a+b=a+b-4\). Hence
\[
a+b=16+4=\boxed{20},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Substituting the root gives an integer part plus an integer multiple of \(\sqrt5\). Irrationality forces both parts to vanish, giving equations for \(a\) and \(b\).

Write \(t=4+\sqrt5\). Its square and cube are
\[
t^2=21+8\sqrt5,
\qquad
t^3=(4+\sqrt5)(21+8\sqrt5)=124+53\sqrt5.
\]
Since \(t\) is a root,
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&=t^3-5t^2+at+b\\
&=(124+53\sqrt5)-5(21+8\sqrt5)+a(4+\sqrt5)+b\\
&=(19+4a+b)+(13+a)\sqrt5.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two coefficients are integers. If \(13+a\ne0\), this equality would express \(\sqrt5\) as a ratio of integers. Thus
\[
13+a=0,
\qquad
19+4a+b=0.
\]
The first equation gives \(a=-13\), and the second gives \(b=33\). Therefore,
\[
a+b=-13+33=\boxed{20},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

criteria: Represent a rational number as an integer numerator over a nonzero integer denominator, including an integer over one. Explain why sums and products retain this form; show that negation preserves it and that a nonzero rational has a rational reciprocal.

Give general arguments for the rational-plus-irrational and nonzero-rational-times-irrational cases using the rational closure and inverse facts to justify reverse subtraction or division. In the product argument, divide only by the nonzero rational multiplier. Explain the zero-factor exception and why the conclusions do not extend to two irrational inputs.
nodes.description: Use integer-fraction representations to justify rational closure under addition and multiplication, and use reverse arithmetic to show that adding a rational to an irrational or multiplying an irrational by a nonzero rational gives an irrational. Justify rational additive inverses and reciprocals of nonzero rationals for these reverse arguments, preserving the nonzero condition.
nodes.name: Rational closure and irrationality under arithmetic
